Q1.answer: The paper investigates whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with its own recent statistics (rolling-window normalization, RWN) reduces forecasting error when the level of a time series shifts after training, without harming accuracy when there is no shift.

Q2.answer: Forecasters deployed on streams such as electricity demand encounter level shifts, and most pipelines normalize inputs with training statistics, which become stale after a shift.
Q2.missing: Citations are marked as needed; the paper does not provide evidence for prevalence or standard practice.

Q3.answer: Existing approaches use fixed training statistics for normalization. Two explanations for shift-induced error compete: stale normalization statistics vs. insufficient model capacity for the new regime. Prior work changed both together, leaving it unclear which factor matters.
Q3.missing: The paper references a literature search not yet run; no specific prior work is cited or described.

Q4.answer: Generated a synthetic hourly series (SynthLoad) with daily/weekly cycles and noise. Trained an MLP (64 hidden units, 168-hour history, 24-hour horizon) on one year. After training, added level shifts of magnitude s ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8} (in training std devs). Compared three normalizations: baseline (training mean/std), RWN (each window normalized by its most recent 48 steps), RWN-fixed (statistics estimated once from first 48 steps post-shift, then frozen). Ran 5 seeds each, reported mean and std of MAE on test period.

Q5.answer: To isolate the effect of normalization statistics from model capacity, they held the model architecture and training budget constant across all three normalization conditions. The 48-step window was chosen in a quick trial and not tuned.
Q5.missing: No rationale for the 48-step window beyond 'quick trial'; no ablation on window length.

Q6.answer: Three normalization conditions × 5 random seeds × 4 shift magnitudes (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8) plus a no-shift condition (s=0). Same MLP, same training budget. MAE measured on test period after shift (or equivalent period for no-shift).
Q6.missing: Details of test period length, training/validation split, and optimization details (lr, epochs, early stopping) are not given.

Q7.answer: No shift: RWN 0.409±0.007 vs baseline 0.412±0.006 (indistinguishable). Shift s=0.6: RWN 0.452 vs baseline 0.641 (29% reduction at this magnitude; 11–29% across s=0.2–0.6). Shift s=0.8: RWN 0.712±0.021 vs baseline 0.731±0.015 (gap ≈1 std dev, no clear benefit). RWN-fixed at s=0.6: 0.518, recovering ~2/3 of RWN's gain.
Q7.missing: Results for s=0.2 and s=0.4 are summarized as '11–29%' but not reported individually.

Q8.answer: In this synthetic setting with a fixed MLP capacity, RWN matches baseline accuracy without shift and substantially reduces MAE under moderate level shifts (s ≤ 0.6). The benefit diminishes at larger shift (s=0.8). A single re-estimation of statistics (RWN-fixed) recovers about two-thirds of RWN's gain at s=0.6, suggesting stale statistics account for much of the baseline's shift-induced error.

Q9.answer: Does not establish: whether RWN works on real data; whether the 48-step window is near-optimal; whether results generalize to other model architectures, horizon lengths, history lengths, shift types (e.g., slope, variance, seasonal changes), or noise levels; whether the ~2/3 attribution to stale statistics holds beyond this one synthetic generator; whether RWN-fixed's single re-estimation is practical (requires detecting shift onset).

Q10.answer: A capacity-controlled comparison showing 11–29% MAE reduction under moderate level shifts at no unshifted cost, a boundary at the largest shift tested (s=0.8), and an ablation (RWN-fixed) attributing about a third of the gain to continued adaptation.

Q11.answer: Single synthetic data generator (SynthLoad); window length (48) not tuned; only level shifts studied; model capacity held constant (not varied); shift detection for RWN-fixed not addressed; no real-world validation; citations for motivation are placeholders.

Q12.answer: Rolling-window normalization (recomputing mean/std per input window) can largely eliminate forecasting degradation from moderate level shifts in a synthetic setting, without hurting no-shift performance, and most of the gain comes from updating statistics rather than continuous adaptation.

objective_discrepancies: Objective states: 'A reader should come away knowing what was tested, what was found, and where the finding stops.' The paper achieves this well; the Conclusion and Limitations jointly define the boundary. Minor discrepancy: the objective mentions 'how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt those statistics' — the paper answers this (~1/3 from continued adaptation via RWN-fixed), but the objective presents it as an open question while the paper treats it as answered.

Objective says the paper 'asks whether normalizing each input window... reduces error... without harming accuracy when there is no shift, and how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt those statistics.' The paper does answer both, but the RQs are only stated in Discussion, not Introduction, so a reader following the objective's framing might expect them earlier.
